claims.claim: Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullianus was born in Carthage around 155‑160 AD and died after 220 AD in the same city.
De spectaculis (On the Shows) was written sometime between 197 and 202 AD.
The treatise examines whether Christians may attend public games, theatres, and gladiatorial spectacles and argues that they should not.
Tertullian claims that the spectacles are steeped in pagan idolatry and that their violent excitement can seduce Christians into sinful bloodlust.
The work is addressed to “Servants of God,” i.e., the Christian community, urging them to consecrate themselves and avoid the pleasures of public shows.
Tertullian wrote the treatise in response to the growing habit of Christians in Carthage and elsewhere still attending the popular public spectacles.
He also refutes the common pagan argument that enjoyment of spectacles is harmless and does not offend God.
De spectaculis survives in Latin manuscripts and has been transmitted through collections such as the Ante‑Nicene Fathers series and modern online editions.
The treatise is an important historical source for the operation of Roman games and for understanding early Christian moral and ascetic teaching.
Later thinkers such as Friedrich Nietzsche cited Tertullian’s vivid description of Christian martyrdom as a substitute for the blood‑sport of the arena.
